plan.topic: Nail changes on GLP-1 medicines (nail lifting/onycholysis, brittleness): EADV 2026 multinational survey, revisited by The Dermatology Digest on Nov 4, 2026
plan.angle: Calm 'Is this normal?' Short. Answer: in a self-reported survey presented at the EADV dermatology congress in October 2026 (not yet peer-reviewed), 39% of GLP-1 medicine users reported nail lifting vs 9% of similar non-users (575 vs 1,329 people). Say 'linked to, not proof'. New fact: about half of users said they had nail problems before starting. Add one line: 'Why isn't known yet. Researchers are still looking.' Mention weight loss or eating less only as an unconfirmed idea. Credit EADV, not a secondary blog. Our own untagged tips: enough protein unless your clinician limits it, and gentle nail care. No supplements. See a doctor or dermatologist for pain, swelling, pus or nails that keep lifting. Include the GI line, 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line.
plan.working_title: GLP-1 Medicines and Your Nails: Is This Normal?
plan.why: It's the proven calm 'Is this normal?' format with a fresh Nov 4 hook and low competition, and the new fact is that many users had nail problems before starting. | fact-check: I verified the core facts. EADV Congress 2026 (Vienna, Sept 30–Oct 3) heard a survey of 575 GLP-1 users vs 1,329 non-users with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity in France, the US, Brazil and Mexico. Nail detachment: 39% vs 9%. About half of users reported nail problems before starting. Nail problems stayed more common even when the analysis was limited to people who had lost weight. That partly weakens a 'fast weight loss' explanation, so if the hypothesis is mentioned it must be worded as the researchers' speculation only. It's a congress abstract and not peer-reviewed: label it so. I didn't verify the Dermatology Digest Nov 4 piece. Credit the EADV congress presentation or the EADV press release instead. Coverage reports the drug class, so keep the title class-level ('GLP-1 medicines') unless the source breaks out tirzepatide.

package.description:
A 2026 survey found nail lifting reported by 39% of GLP-1 users with type 2 diabetes or obesity, vs 9% of non-users with those conditions. It's self-reported, not yet peer-reviewed, and weight loss alone didn't explain the gap.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: The science is accurate. I checked it against the EADV press release, HCPLive, Medical Xpress and EMJ Reviews. 575 GLP-1 users were compared with 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity who had never taken the drugs, recruited in France, the US, Brazil and Mexico. Nail detachment was reported by 39% of users vs 9% of controls. "Around half of users reported nail problems before starting treatment" is confirmed, and so is the point that differences stayed significant among people who had lost weight. The study was cross-sectional and self-reported, presented at EADV 2026 in Vienna, with no peer-reviewed paper yet. The caveats are honest ("linked to, not proof", self-reported, cause unknown). Safety is covered: there's a when-to-get-checked line, the don't-stop line, the protein caveat for people whose clinician limits protein, "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line. Our own tips carry no source tags. The word count is exactly 170. Both label PDFs (Zepbound, Wegovy) load. I couldn't extract their text, but "stomach issues are the most common side effects" matches the well-known adverse-reaction sections of both labels. The only issues are minor precision fixes, and the word count stays at 170 or under once they're applied.
